0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Book of Leviticus
0.overview:
Leviticus is the book most Christians skip and most preachers fear. Its pages drip with blood, smoke, and the minute regulation of altars, animals, and ailments. Yet to neglect Leviticus is to neglect the very heart of the gospel, for here, more than anywhere in the Old Testament, we learn how a sinful people may dwell with a holy God. The whole book answers a single question raised at the end of Exodus: when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle so that even Moses could not enter (Exod 40:35), how shall mortal, defiled creatures come near? Leviticus is God's gracious answer — a manual of access, written in the language of sacrifice.

The dominating word is holy. It appears more often in Leviticus than in any other book of the Bible. As R.C. Sproul never tired of insisting, holiness is not merely one of God's attributes among many; it is the very burning core of his being. The seraphim do not cry "Love, love, love" or "Mercy, mercy, mercy," but "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3). Leviticus exists to brand that threefold cry upon the conscience of a redeemed people: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2).

But Leviticus is not legalism. It stands inside grace. Israel is already redeemed; the blood of the Passover lamb has already been shed; the people have already been brought out of Egypt and into covenant at Sinai. Everything in Leviticus is for a people God has already claimed as his own. The sacrifices do not purchase God's love — they are the appointed means by which an already-loved people may live in the presence of the One who loves them. Grace precedes law, as it always does.

Above all, Leviticus is about Jesus. Every offering, every priest, every drop of blood, every Day of Atonement points beyond itself to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The book of Hebrews is the inspired commentary on Leviticus, and its message is that all these shadows have found their substance in Christ. To read Leviticus rightly is to be brought, again and again, to the foot of the cross and to whisper with adoring wonder, "It is finished." Holy, holy, holy — and yet, in Christ, the holy God has made a way for us to come home.

1.title: The Burnt Offering: Wholly the Lord's
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, <sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD... <sup>4</sup>He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. <sup>9</sup>...And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD."
1.overview:
Leviticus opens not with a command but with a calling: "The LORD called Moses." The same God whose glory had just filled the tabernacle now speaks from within it, and his first word to a redeemed people is about worship — how to draw near. The very first offering described is the burnt offering, the 'olah, the offering that ascends. It is the only sacrifice in which the entire animal, apart from the skin, is consumed upon the altar. Nothing is held back; nothing is eaten by priest or worshipper. It goes up entirely to God in smoke.

Gordon Wenham observes that the burnt offering is fundamentally an offering of total self-dedication. The worshipper is saying, in the language of fire, "All that I am I give to you." The key gesture is in verse 4: the worshipper lays his hand upon the head of the animal. This is the language of identification and substitution. As the hand presses down, the worshipper's guilt is symbolically transferred; what happens to the animal happens, by representation, to the man. The innocent dies in place of the guilty.

Sinclair Ferguson reminds us that the phrase "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" is not crude anthropomorphism but covenant language: the sacrifice is acceptable, it satisfies, it brings delight to the heart of God. And here the gospel breaks through, for Paul takes this very phrase and applies it to Christ: "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2).

The burnt offering is Christ our whole burnt offering — the one who held nothing back, who gave himself entirely to the Father on our behalf, who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7). Where our consecration is always partial, hesitant, hedged with reservations, his was total. He ascended in the flame of the Father's will and rose as the fragrance that makes us, in him, acceptable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The God Who Calls and the Worship He Commands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks from the tent of meeting, initiating worship. True worship is never invented by us; it is revealed by him. The offerings come from the herd or the flock, from the worshipper's own livelihood.
verseByVerse.theology: Worship is God-initiated and God-regulated. The Reformed regulative principle is born here: we worship not as we please but as God prescribes.
verseByVerse.examples: We do not get to design our own approach to God. The way to him is the way he appoints, and that way is finally a Person, Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary: The book begins mid-sentence in the Hebrew, joined to Exodus by a single connecting word: and. Leviticus is the continuation of the story of redemption. Calvin notes that God, having filled the tent with his glory, does not leave his people in terror but graciously speaks, opening a way of access. The Voice from the tent is the mercy of a holy God who will not abandon his people to the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary: The offering must cost something; it comes from the worshipper's own herd, his livelihood, his life. Begg often presses the point that worship which costs us nothing is worth nothing. David said it plainly: "I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing" (2 Sam 24:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–9 — The Bull: Substitution and Ascent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worshipper brings a male without blemish, lays his hand on its head, and it is accepted to make atonement. The animal is slaughtered, its blood thrown against the altar, and the whole is burned as a pleasing aroma.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitutionary atonement is the beating heart of biblical religion. The blameless dies for the blemished; the laid-on hand transfers guilt.
verseByVerse.examples: Every time we trust Christ we lay our hand by faith upon the head of the true Lamb, and what happened to him counts as having happened to us.

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Without blemish" — the demand for perfection runs through the whole sacrificial system and finds its terminus in the One whom Peter calls "a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19). No flawed substitute will do. Only a perfect life can stand in the place of forfeit lives.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the gospel in a gesture. The hand pressed upon the head is the visible sermon of substitution. Keller put it memorably: the essence of the gospel is that God treated Jesus as we deserve, that he might treat us as Jesus deserved. The worshipper does not climb to God by his goodness; he lays his hand on another and is "accepted." Atonement — kipper, to cover, to ransom, to wipe away — is made not by the sinner's effort but by the substitute's death.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary: The worshipper himself wields the knife. He must feel the weight of what sin costs — that a life is forfeit, that blood must flow. Sproul insisted that the sheer bloodiness of Old Testament worship was meant to horrify, to teach a complacent heart that the wages of sin is death.

verseByVerse.quote: ...And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: "All of it." This is the distinctive of the burnt offering — total consumption, total surrender. Wenham notes that the burnt offering, more than any other, expresses entire devotion. It is the picture of Christ who gave himself wholly, and the pattern of the believer who, in view of God's mercies, presents his body "a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God" (Rom 12:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Flock and the Bird: Grace for the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Provision is made for those of lesser means — a sheep or goat, or even two birds. The same atonement is available regardless of wealth.
verseByVerse.theology: The accessibility of atonement: God scales the offering to the worshipper's means so that no one is shut out by poverty.
verseByVerse.examples: The ground is level at the foot of the altar. The same Christ who saves the rich saves the poor; salvation cannot be bought, only received.

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons.
verseByVerse.commentary: The bird offering is the poor person's burnt offering — the very offering Mary and Joseph would later bring for the infant Jesus (Luke 2:24). The Lord of glory entered the world among those who could afford only the offering of the poor. Grace stoops low.

1.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The laid-on hand and the slain victim teach that sin is dealt with not by human effort but by a divinely provided substitute. This is the spine of biblical religion and the heart of the cross.

Total consecration. The wholly consumed offering models the surrender Christ rendered to the Father and which the Spirit now works in us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).

The pleasing aroma. What the burnt offering symbolized, Christ accomplished — he is "a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2), and in him our worship rises acceptably.
1.examples:
Then: An Israelite, conscious of sin, brought a bull from his own herd, pressed his hand upon its head, and watched it die and ascend in flame — a vivid, costly, bloody lesson that approaching God requires a substitute.

Now: We come to God through the once-for-all offering of Christ. The burnt offering calls us to a worship that holds nothing back — to lay our whole selves on the altar, knowing we are already accepted in the Beloved.

2.title: The Grain Offering: The Labor of Our Hands
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it... <sup>11</sup>No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD. <sup>13</sup>You shall season all your grain offerings with salt... the salt of the covenant with your God.
2.overview:
After the bloody burnt offering comes the bloodless grain offering, the minchah — a gift, a tribute. Where the burnt offering speaks of atonement, the grain offering speaks of consecrated labor. Grain does not grow wild and ready; it is the product of plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding. To bring fine flour is to bring the fruit of one's toil, the offering of one's working life laid upon the altar of God.

Wenham notes that the grain offering often accompanied the burnt offering, so that the dedication of the self (the burnt offering) was joined to the dedication of the self's labor (the grain offering). The God who redeems us claims not only our souls but our Mondays — our work, our wages, our ordinary industry.

Three details preach. No leaven, for leaven, the fermenting agent of corruption, is throughout Scripture a symbol of sin (1 Cor 5:8). No honey, for the sweetness of the world's natural fermentation has no place on God's altar. But salt — "the salt of the covenant" — must season every offering, for salt preserves, salt does not corrupt, salt seals a covenant as an enduring bond.

And here is Christ, the true bread offered to the Father. He is the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died (John 12:24); he is the bread of life (John 6:35); his was the only human life ever lived wholly without the leaven of sin, seasoned through and through with the salt of unbreakable covenant faithfulness. The grain offering, ground fine and passed through fire, whispers of the One whose perfect life of labor and obedience was offered up, a pleasing aroma, for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Fine Flour, Oil, and Frankincense
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The grain offering is fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense. A memorial portion is burned; the rest belongs to the priests.
verseByVerse.theology: The dedication of human labor to God. Worship encompasses the whole of life, not merely the religious sphere.
verseByVerse.examples: Our daily work, offered to God, becomes worship. The Christian does not divide life into sacred and secular; all is offered up.

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fine flour required grinding — the patient, costly transformation of raw grain into something fit for the altar. Begg notes that there is a kind of grinding in every faithful life, a crushing of self that yields an offering fit for God. The oil speaks of the Spirit; the frankincense, of prayer ascending sweetly (Ps 141:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests, and he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary: A "memorial portion" rises to God while the rest sustains the priests. Calvin observes the beautiful economy: God claims his share, and in the same act provides for his servants. Our giving to God is never lost; it feeds his ministers and ascends to his throne.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — No Leaven, No Honey, but Salt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaven and honey, agents of fermentation and decay, are forbidden. Salt, the preservative and sign of covenant, is required on every offering.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness excludes corruption. The covenant is a bond of salt — enduring, incorruptible, faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus calls us 'the salt of the earth' (Matt 5:13). The covenant people are to be a preserving, incorruptible presence in a decaying world.

verseByVerse.quote: No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Leaven works secretly, spreading through the whole lump — the perfect emblem of sin. Paul applies it directly: "Cleanse out the old leaven... For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Let us therefore celebrate the festival... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:7–8). On God's altar there is no place for the corruption of sin.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The salt of the covenant" — a covenant of salt is one that does not spoil (Num 18:19). It binds the parties in enduring faithfulness. Christ keeps the covenant of salt unbroken on our behalf, and bids us, "Have salt in yourselves" (Mark 9:50) — to be people whose faithfulness does not corrupt.

2.theology:
Consecrated work. The fruit of human labor, offered to God, becomes worship. There is no merely secular work for the believer; all is dedicated to the Lord.

The exclusion of corruption. No leaven, no honey — holiness admits no fermenting agent of sin. Christ alone was utterly unleavened, the sinless bread offered to God.

The covenant of salt. The enduring, incorruptible faithfulness of God's covenant, kept perfectly by Christ and reflected in a people called to be salt.
2.examples:
Then: The Israelite farmer brought the ground fruit of his fields, seasoned with salt, free of leaven — dedicating the produce of his labor to the God who gave the increase.

Now: We offer our work, our wages, our ordinary toil to God as worship. And we look to Christ, the true bread, the grain of wheat that died to bring forth much fruit.

3.title: The Peace Offering: Communion Restored
3.text: <sup>1</sup>If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering... <sup>5</sup>...a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. <sup>16</sup>...All fat is the LORD's. <sup>17</sup>It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood.
3.overview:
The peace offering, the shelamim — from the great word shalom — is the offering of fellowship, of communion, of restored relationship. It is unique among the sacrifices in that the worshipper eats it. After God receives the fat and the priests their portion, the offerer and his household sit down to a sacred meal in the presence of God. This is the only sacrifice that ends in a feast.

Wenham points out that the peace offering celebrates the reconciliation that the other offerings make possible. The burnt offering atones; the peace offering rejoices. Here is the goal of all sacrifice: not merely the removal of guilt but the restoration of communion, table-fellowship with the living God. Sin had banished man from God's presence; the peace offering brings him back to the table.

The fat and the blood belong to God alone — the fat as the richest portion, the choicest part reserved for him, and the blood because it is the life, sacred and not to be consumed. The worshipper learns that even in joyful fellowship, God is God; the best is his.

And Christ is our peace (Eph 2:14). "Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1). The peace offering anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled people of God sit down to eat in his presence, sharing in the body and blood of the one whose sacrifice made peace "by the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). Every Communion is a peace-offering feast — the celebration meal of those brought home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Offering from the Herd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The peace offering may be male or female, without blemish. The hand is laid on its head; the fat is burned to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Reconciliation issues in fellowship. The peace offering celebrates restored communion with God.
verseByVerse.examples: The end of the gospel is not merely pardon but fellowship — being welcomed back to God's table as a beloved child.

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Notably, male or female is accepted — the peace offering is the most inclusive of sacrifices, fitting for an offering of joy and thanksgiving open to all the reconciled. Ferguson highlights that shalom is not mere absence of conflict but the fullness of flourishing in God's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering... a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The peace offering is laid "on top of the burnt offering." Fellowship rests upon atonement. There can be no feast of communion that does not stand upon the foundation of a substitute already slain. So our peace with God rests wholly on the finished work of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — All Fat Is the Lord's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fat and the blood are forbidden to the worshipper; the fat is the LORD's choicest portion, the blood is the sacred life.
verseByVerse.theology: God claims the best. The reservation of fat and blood teaches that even in our joy, God receives the choicest and the life is his.
verseByVerse.examples: We give God not our leftovers but our first and best — our prime time, our finest energies, the fat of our lives.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary: "All fat is the LORD's." The richest, choicest portion is reserved for God. Calvin draws the lesson that God will not be served with the dregs but claims the best of all we have. Begg presses it home: do we give God the fat, or the scraps?

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood.
verseByVerse.commentary: The prohibition of blood points forward to ch. 17 and to the whole theology of atonement: the life is in the blood, and the blood is sacred to God. Only One had the right to pour out his blood as the price of peace, and he did — "making peace by the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20).

3.theology:
Peace with God. The reconciliation accomplished by atonement issues in restored fellowship — the very heart of shalom, fulfilled in Christ "who is our peace" (Eph 2:14).

The fellowship meal. The shared meal anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled feast in God's presence on the body and blood of Christ.

God's claim on the best. The fat belongs to the LORD — God receives the choicest portion, not the leftovers.
3.examples:
Then: An Israelite family, reconciled to God, sat down to a joyful sacred meal in his courts, the fat ascending to God, the meat shared in fellowship and thanksgiving.

Now: At the Lord's Table we celebrate the peace Christ made by his blood. The peace offering teaches us that the gospel's goal is not mere pardon but feasting fellowship with our God.

4.title: The Sin Offering: Even Unintended Sin
4.text: <sup>2</sup>...If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them... <sup>3</sup>if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people... <sup>20</sup>...and the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
4.overview:
Now the tone deepens. The burnt, grain, and peace offerings were largely voluntary expressions of devotion. The sin offering, the chatta't, is mandatory — it deals with the dreadful fact of guilt. And its first and most arresting lesson is this: it is provided for sins committed unintentionally. Sins we never noticed, never meant, never even knew we were committing — these too defile, these too require blood.

Sproul drove this home with terrifying clarity: we so easily measure sin by our intentions, but God measures it by his holiness. The sin offering teaches that guilt is not chiefly a matter of malice but of contamination. Even the sin we stumble into unawares pollutes the sanctuary and bars us from God. If unintentional sin is this serious, what shall we say of the high-handed, deliberate rebellions of our hearts?

The chapter is structured by a striking gradation of rank. The anointed priest, the whole congregation, the leader, the common person — each requires an offering, and the higher the office, the costlier the sacrifice. The priest and the congregation require a bull; the leader a male goat; the common person a female goat or lamb. Leadership carries greater accountability before God.

And here Christ bears the sins of the whole people. He is the sin offering — "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21). The blood of the sin offering was taken into the Holy Place; Christ entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, bearing not the unintentional sins of one man but the mountainous, deliberate sins of a countless multitude. "They shall be forgiven" — the most beautiful refrain in the chapter — is purchased for us at infinite cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Sin of the Anointed Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the high priest sins, he brings guilt on the people; he must offer a bull, sprinkle blood before the veil, and burn the carcass outside the camp.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the holiest leader sins and needs atonement. The sin of leaders has corporate consequences.
verseByVerse.examples: Spiritual leaders are not above sin; their failures wound the whole community. All the more, we need a sinless High Priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them,
verseByVerse.commentary: "Unintentionally" — Wenham notes the Hebrew covers sins of inadvertence, ignorance, and weakness. The point is staggering: sin we never intended still requires blood. Our guilt runs deeper than our awareness of it. As David prayed, "Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults" (Ps 19:12).

verseByVerse.quote: if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering.
verseByVerse.commentary: The priest's sin "brings guilt on the people" — leadership is representative, and its failures are contagious. Begg observes the sobering weight upon those who lead God's people: their stumbling damages many. Israel's priests sinned and needed offerings for themselves; how we need Christ, the High Priest "who has no need... to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins" (Heb 7:27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sin of the Whole Congregation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the whole assembly sins unwittingly, the elders lay hands on a bull, atonement is made, and they are forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology: Corporate sin and corporate atonement. A whole community can drift into guilt and needs collective cleansing.
verseByVerse.examples: Churches and nations sin corporately. We need both personal and corporate repentance before a holy God.

verseByVerse.quote: ...Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: "And they shall be forgiven." Here is the sweetest word in Leviticus. The whole bloody apparatus exists to make this sentence possible. Calvin marveled that God should bind himself to forgive upon the offering of a substitute. The shadow becomes substance at Calvary, where the blood of Christ secures forgiveness not for a season but forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–35 — The Leader and the Common Person
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A leader brings a male goat; a common person a female goat or lamb. Each receives atonement and forgiveness.
verseByVerse.theology: Atonement is graded by means and accountability, yet available to all. No one is too lowly to be forgiven.
verseByVerse.examples: From the highest leader to the humblest peasant, all stand guilty and all may be forgiven through the appointed sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,
verseByVerse.commentary: "And realizes his guilt" — the awakening of conscience precedes the bringing of the offering. The Spirit's first work is to make us know our guilt. Sproul: until we see our sin against the backdrop of God's holiness, we will never run to the sacrifice. Conviction is mercy's herald.

4.theology:
The gravity of unintentional sin. Sin defiles whether or not we intend it; guilt is measured by God's holiness, not our awareness. This shatters self-righteousness.

Graded accountability. The higher the office, the costlier the offering — leadership carries greater responsibility before God (cf. James 3:1).

'They shall be forgiven.' The refrain of grace. Christ the sin offering secures the forgiveness the bulls and goats could only foreshadow (2 Cor 5:21; Heb 10:4).
4.examples:
Then: An Israelite, suddenly conscious of a sin he had committed unawares, brought a goat, laid his hand on its head, and heard the priest pronounce him forgiven.

Now: We are guiltier than we know — but in Christ, more loved than we dared hope. The sin offering drives us to the cross, where the deepest, most hidden guilt is fully and finally covered.

5.title: The Guilt Offering: Forgiveness and Restoration
5.text: <sup>5</sup>...when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed... <sup>15</sup>If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD... he shall make restitution... and shall add a fifth to it. <sup>16</sup>...and the priest shall make atonement for him... and he shall be forgiven.
5.overview:
The guilt offering, the 'asham (also called the reparation offering), overlaps with the sin offering but adds a vital dimension: restitution. Where a sin has caused measurable loss — a debt to God's holy things or a fraud against a neighbor — the guilty party must not only bring a sacrifice but make full restitution, adding a fifth. Forgiveness does not float free of repair. Grace does not excuse us from making things right; it empowers us to.

This is the offering that demands confession (5:5) — the open naming of sin before God. And it is the offering that joins atonement to amendment, the altar to the ledger. The reconciled sinner returns the stolen, repays the defrauded, and adds twenty percent on top. Zacchaeus, climbing down from his tree to give back fourfold (Luke 19:8), is a son of the guilt offering, transformed by grace into a maker of restitution.

Wenham observes the moral seriousness here: God cares not only that we feel forgiven but that the web of relationships torn by our sin be rewoven. The guilt offering refuses cheap grace.

And Christ is the One who not only forgives but restores. Isaiah 53:10 says, "when his soul makes an offering for guilt" — the suffering Servant is himself the 'asham. He pays not only the principal of our debt but the added fifth and infinitely more, restoring to God a glory greater than Adam lost, and restoring to us a sonship richer than Eden. He gives back what he never took away (Ps 69:4). The guilt offering points to a Savior who does not merely cancel our debt but rebuilds what sin demolished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Various cases of incurred guilt — withheld testimony, contact with uncleanness, rash oaths. The guilty must confess and bring an offering.
verseByVerse.theology: Confession is the gateway to forgiveness. Sin must be named, not minimized.
verseByVerse.examples: 'If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive' (1 John 1:9). Naming sin honestly is the path to cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed,
verseByVerse.commentary: "And confesses" — here confession enters the sacrificial system explicitly. Ferguson notes that true repentance always involves the specific, honest naming of sin. We do not confess in vague generalities; we name the thing, own it, and bring it to the altar. Concealment kills; confession heals (Prov 28:13).

verseByVerse.quote: and he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: Confession and sacrifice go together — words alone do not atone; blood must flow. Yet the merciful gradation continues into the following verses, where the poor may bring two birds, and the very poor a tenth of an ephah of flour (vv. 7, 11). No one is shut out from atonement by poverty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For breaches involving the LORD's holy things, the guilty makes restitution, adds a fifth, and brings a ram. Atonement is made and he is forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology: Forgiveness includes repair. Grace empowers restitution; it does not bypass it.
verseByVerse.examples: True repentance restores what sin has stolen. Zacchaeus gives back fourfold; the forgiven heart makes things right.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock... for a guilt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary: "A breach of faith" — the Hebrew suggests treachery, a betrayal of trust. Sin against God's holy things is covenant unfaithfulness. Calvin underscores that to rob God of his due is no small matter; it is faithlessness against the One who gave us all things.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: Restitution plus a fifth — repentance overpays. The forgiven sinner is so transformed that he gives back more than he took. And here we glimpse Christ, the true guilt offering of Isaiah 53:10, who restores to God more glory and to us more grace than sin ever stole. "He shall be forgiven" — purchased by the blood of the spotless Ram of God.

5.theology:
Confession. Sin must be named openly before God. The guilt offering enshrines confession as the gateway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

Restitution. Grace does not bypass repair; it empowers it. The forgiven make things right, even adding a fifth — repentance overpays.

Christ our restorer. The suffering Servant is himself the guilt offering (Isa 53:10), who does not merely forgive but restores, giving back what he never took away (Ps 69:4).
5.examples:
Then: An Israelite who had defrauded another or robbed God's holy things confessed, repaid the loss with a fifth added, and brought a ram — his repentance bearing fruit in restored relationships.

Now: Real repentance still makes restitution. And we rest in Christ, the guilt offering who not only cancels our debt but rebuilds everything sin destroyed.

6.title: Laws for the Priests: The Fire That Never Goes Out
6.text: <sup>12</sup>The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning... <sup>13</sup>Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
6.overview:
Chapters 6 and 7 turn from the worshipper's instructions to the priests' instructions — the administrative regulations for handling each offering. This may seem the dustiest corner of Leviticus, yet it glows with quiet glory. The God who is a consuming fire orders his worship down to the disposal of ashes, because nothing about approaching him is trivial.

The towering image of chapter 6 is the perpetual fire: "Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out" (6:13). Twice the command is repeated. The flame that first fell from God himself (9:24) was never to be allowed to die. The priests fed it every morning. It burned through the night. It was the visible sign that atonement was always available, that the door to God never closed, that the fire of his presence and the fire of sacrifice burned on, unceasing.

Begg loves to draw the line to the believer's heart: there is a fire that must never go out, a devotion fed morning by morning, a flame of love for God tended daily lest it gutter into cold ash. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). The Reformers spoke of the daily mortification of sin and the daily stoking of grace — the morning wood laid on the altar of the heart.

Above all, the perpetual fire foreshadows the perpetual efficacy of Christ's sacrifice. The altar fire never went out because Israel sinned without ceasing and needed atonement without ceasing. But Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb 10:12). The one offering that need never be repeated has made the endless fire unnecessary — yet the devotion it symbolized burns brighter than ever in hearts set aflame by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Law of the Burnt Offering and the Perpetual Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priest tends the burnt offering through the night, removes the ashes reverently, and keeps the altar fire burning continually.
verseByVerse.theology: The continual fire signifies continual atonement and unceasing devotion. God's worship is to be tended, not neglected.
verseByVerse.examples: The flame of devotion must be fed daily. Spiritual fire dies not by one great sin but by slow neglect.

verseByVerse.quote: The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Every morning" — the priest's first daily task was to feed the fire. There is a daily discipline to keeping the heart aflame. Calvin notes that God will be worshipped without intermission; lukewarmness is an affront to the consuming fire.

verseByVerse.quote: Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
verseByVerse.commentary: The double repetition stamps the command on the memory. Sproul saw here the unceasing nature of Israel's need: the fire could not go out because sin did not stop. How glorious, then, that Christ's one offering ended the need for the endless flame — and how fitting that the Spirit now keeps an unquenchable fire burning in the church (Acts 2:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — The Grain Offering and the Priests' Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Regulations for the grain offering, the priests' share, and the high priest's daily grain offering wholly burned.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who serve at the altar live by the altar — God provides for his ministers.
verseByVerse.examples: 'The laborer deserves his wages' (1 Tim 5:18). God ordains that his servants be supported by the people they serve.

verseByVerse.quote: Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Whatever touches them shall become holy" — holiness here is contagious, communicated by contact. This is the inverse of the uncleanness that spreads by touch in chapters 11–15. In Christ, holiness becomes the contagion: he touches lepers and the dead and makes them clean (Mark 5; Luke 17). Begg notes that in the old order, defilement spread; in the new, the Holy One spreads life.

6.theology:
The perpetual fire. The unceasing altar flame signified the constant availability of atonement and the constant need of a sinful people — a need answered once for all in Christ (Heb 10:12).

Daily devotion. The morning wood on the altar pictures the discipline of tending the heart's fire lest it grow cold. 'Do not quench the Spirit' (1 Thess 5:19).

Provision for ministers. Those who serve at the altar share in the altar; God provides for his servants through the offerings of his people.
6.examples:
Then: Before dawn the priest stirred the embers, laid on fresh wood, and removed the night's ashes — guarding the flame God himself had kindled so that it never died.

Now: We tend the fire of devotion daily by the Word, prayer, and the Spirit. And we rest in the finished sacrifice that ended the need for endless offerings, even as our hearts burn within us (Luke 24:32).

7.title: The Portion of the Priests: Order in Holy Things
7.text: <sup>11</sup>And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD... <sup>26</sup>You shall not eat any blood whatever, whether of bird or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. <sup>34</sup>...I have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 completes the priestly handbook, covering the guilt offering, the peace offering, and the assignment of the priests' portions. To modern ears these are dry logistics; to the eye of faith they reveal the beauty of God's ordered worship. "God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33). The meticulous care given to who eats what, when, and how, teaches that the worship of a holy God is never careless or improvised.

The peace offering is here divided into thanksgiving, vow, and freewill varieties (7:12–16), with the thanksgiving offering to be eaten the same day — joy is not to be hoarded but shared while it is fresh. The breast and the right thigh are assigned to the priests as their "wave offering" and "contribution" (7:30–34), God's gracious provision for those who serve.

Twice more the prohibition of blood and fat is pressed (7:22–27). The blood belongs to God because the life is in it; to eat blood is to seize what is sacred to the Lord alone. This single principle — that blood is life and life is God's — will become the explicit theology of chapter 17 and the foundation of all that Hebrews says about the blood of Christ.

The whole chapter exalts the orderliness of grace. Carson reminds us that the God who saves is the God who orders; redemption is not chaos but the careful, costly, beautiful arrangement of holy things. And every portion reserved, every drop of blood withheld, every wave of the priest's hands points to the day when the perfect Priest would offer the perfect sacrifice and assign to his people the choicest portion of all — himself, the bread and the cup of the new covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Law of the Peace Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peace offerings of thanksgiving, vow, and freewill are regulated. The thanksgiving meal must be eaten the same day; uncleanness disqualifies the eater.
verseByVerse.theology: Thanksgiving is to be expressed promptly and joyfully; holiness governs even the fellowship meal.
verseByVerse.examples: Gratitude shared while fresh blesses the whole community. We must not let thankfulness grow stale.

verseByVerse.quote: If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil...
verseByVerse.commentary: The thanksgiving offering — todah — is the joyful response to deliverance, the sacrifice of praise. Hebrews 13:15 transposes it into a new key: "Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God." Our thanksgiving rises now through Christ, the fruit of lips that confess his name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Prohibition of Fat and Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is forbidden to eat the fat or the blood of sacrificial animals; the fat is God's, the blood is the sacred life.
verseByVerse.theology: The life is in the blood and belongs to God. This principle undergirds the whole theology of atonement.
verseByVerse.examples: The sacredness of life and blood prepares us to grasp the infinite worth of the blood of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not eat any blood whatever, whether of bird or of animal, in any of your dwelling places.
verseByVerse.commentary: The blood is reserved, untouchable, because it is life and life is God's gift and God's claim. Sproul saw in this reverence a preparation for the cross: when at last blood was poured out that we were invited not to shun but to drink — "this is my blood" (Matt 26:28) — the unthinkable had happened. The blood once forbidden became the blood of life eternal.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The breast (wave offering) and right thigh (contribution) are given to the priests as a perpetual due.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides for his ministers from the offerings; service at the altar is honored with a share of the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: The church is to support those who labor in the Word. God ordains generous provision for his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's provision for the priests is built into the very structure of worship. Paul cites this principle: "those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple... the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel" (1 Cor 9:13–14). Grace orders generosity.

7.theology:
The order of worship. God's meticulous regulation of holy things reflects that he is 'not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor 14:33). Redemption is ordered, not chaotic.

The sanctity of blood. The life is in the blood, and the blood belongs to God — the foundation of atonement theology fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. The todah offering becomes, in Christ, the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
7.examples:
Then: The reconciled Israelite shared a thanksgiving feast the same day, the priests received the breast and thigh, and not a drop of blood was consumed — every detail ordered by God.

Now: We offer the sacrifice of praise through Christ, support those who serve God's people, and marvel that the blood once forbidden is now, in Christ, the cup of salvation.

8.title: The Ordination of Aaron: Consecrated by Blood and Oil
8.text: <sup>12</sup>And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him. <sup>23</sup>...and Moses... put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. <sup>30</sup>...and consecrated Aaron and his garments...
8.overview:
From the laws of sacrifice we turn to the consecration of those who will administer them. Chapters 8–10 form the great narrative center of the offering section: the ordination of Aaron and his sons, their first ministry, and the catastrophe that follows. Chapter 8 is the seven-day investiture of the priesthood, carried out by Moses, who here acts as the presiding priest, mediating the very mediators.

The ritual is rich with gospel symbol. Aaron is washed with water (8:6) — the cleansing every minister of God needs. He is clothed in the glorious garments (8:7–9), arrayed not in his own righteousness but in robes provided. He is anointed with oil (8:12), set apart by the Spirit's symbol. And he is marked with blood on the ear, the thumb, and the toe (8:23) — the whole man, hearing, working, walking, consecrated to God by sacrifice.

Wenham notes the sevenfold sprinkling and the seven days of waiting (8:33–35): the number of completeness, the patient setting-apart of those who would draw near to God. Aaron could not appoint himself; he was called, washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. "No one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was" (Heb 5:4).

And all of it anticipates Christ's consecration. At his baptism the sinless Son went down into the water, and the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father spoke — the true Aaron washed and anointed for his priestly work (Matt 3:16–17; Acts 10:38). Yet how the contrast dazzles: Aaron needed blood applied to himself for his own sin; Christ needed no cleansing, but became himself the blood of consecration. He is at once the Priest who is anointed and the sacrifice whose blood consecrates. The ear that perfectly heard the Father, the hands that only did good, the feet that never strayed — wholly consecrated, he ordains us "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses washes Aaron and his sons, clothes them in the priestly garments, and anoints Aaron and the tabernacle with oil.
verseByVerse.theology: Priesthood is conferred, not seized — cleansing, clothing, and anointing all come from outside the man.
verseByVerse.examples: We are made priests to God not by our own worthiness but by being washed, clothed in Christ's righteousness, and anointed by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water.
verseByVerse.commentary: The priest begins with washing — even the holiest service requires cleansing. Titus 3:5 echoes it: "he saved us... by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit." No one ministers to God uncleansed; grace washes before it commissions.

verseByVerse.quote: And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The oil poured on the head — "like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron" (Ps 133:2). Ferguson connects this to the Spirit who anointed Christ (the Anointed One, Messiah) and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20). The fragrant oil running down is the picture of the Spirit poured out on the church's Head and flowing to every member.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–30 — The Sacrifices and the Blood of Consecration
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A sin offering, burnt offering, and ram of ordination are offered. Blood is put on the priests' ear, thumb, and toe, and sprinkled with oil on them and their garments.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole person is consecrated by blood — hearing, doing, walking all set apart to God through sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Christ consecrates our whole life: ears to hear his Word, hands to do his work, feet to walk in his ways.

verseByVerse.quote: And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.
verseByVerse.commentary: Blood on ear, thumb, and toe — the whole man consecrated through sacrifice. Begg observes that nothing is left unclaimed: the ear that hears God, the hand that serves him, the foot that walks his paths. And the order is striking: the blood comes first, before the oil (8:30). The Spirit's anointing rests upon a life first claimed by atoning blood. So too for us — Christ's blood before the Spirit's filling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron and his sons remain at the tent for seven days, keeping the LORD's charge, lest they die.
verseByVerse.theology: Consecration requires patient waiting and obedience. Drawing near to God is no light or hasty thing.
verseByVerse.examples: Spiritual readiness for service is cultivated over time, in obedience and waiting upon God.

verseByVerse.quote: At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die...
verseByVerse.commentary: "So that you do not die" — a solemn note that anticipates the tragedy of chapter 10. Drawing near to a holy God is a matter of life and death. The seven days of patient obedience underscore that priesthood is not a casual privilege but a fearful trust. Calvin: God's servants must learn reverence before they presume to minister.

8.theology:
Priesthood conferred from outside. Aaron is washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. No one takes this honor for himself (Heb 5:4); so we are made priests by grace.

Whole-life consecration. Blood on ear, hand, and foot claims the entire person for God — fulfilled as Christ consecrates every faculty of those he saves.

The anointing of the Spirit. The oil poured on Aaron foreshadows the Spirit who anointed Christ at his baptism and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20; Acts 10:38).
8.examples:
Then: For seven days Moses washed, robed, anointed, and blooded Aaron and his sons, setting apart Israel's priesthood with patient, fearful reverence.

Now: Christ, washed and anointed at his baptism, is our consecrated High Priest, and by his blood and Spirit he makes us 'a royal priesthood' (1 Pet 2:9), our whole lives set apart for God.

9.title: The Glory Appears: Fire from Heaven
9.text: <sup>6</sup>And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." <sup>23</sup>...and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. <sup>24</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering... and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
9.overview:
The seven days of preparation are over; the eighth day dawns. Aaron, newly consecrated, offers his first sacrifices — first for himself, then for the people. The whole drama drives toward a single promised climax: "that the glory of the LORD may appear to you" (9:6). All the offerings, all the blood, all the careful ritual aim at this — that sinners might behold the glory of God and live.

And the glory comes. When Aaron and Moses bless the people, "the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people" (9:23). Then fire — the holy fire of God's own presence — flashes out and consumes the offering on the altar. This is heaven's amen, God's visible acceptance of the sacrifice, the divine seal upon the whole sacrificial system. The God who is a consuming fire consumes the substitute and spares the people.

The response is the only fitting one: "when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces" (9:24). Joy and awe, ecstasy and prostration, together. This is worship in the presence of glory — not the casual familiarity of a trifling age but the trembling, exultant adoration of those who have seen the fire fall and lived. Sproul often said that the proper response to the holiness of God is to fall on our faces; here Israel does exactly that, even as they shout for joy.

The fire that fell on the altar fell, at the last, on Christ. At Calvary the consuming fire of God's holiness fell upon the true sacrifice, and he was wholly consumed in our place. And because the fire fell on him, it need never fall on us. The glory that Israel glimpsed for a moment now shines "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), and we who behold it are summoned to the same response: shouting joy and prostrate awe before the God who accepts us in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the eighth day Aaron offers a sin offering and burnt offering for himself, that he might be fit to minister for the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest must atone for his own sin before mediating for others — pointing to the need of a sinless priest.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who would lead others to God must first deal with their own sin. Yet we have a High Priest who needed no offering for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the goal of all worship stated in a sentence: "that the glory of the LORD may appear." Begg notes that the aim of every ordinance, every sacrifice, every act of obedience is the manifestation of God's glory. Worship is not finally about us; it is about the appearing of his glory, which is our deepest joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people..."
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron must first atone "for yourself." The contrast with Christ is the whole argument of Hebrews: our High Priest is "holy, innocent, unstained" and "has no need... to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins" (Heb 7:26–27). Aaron's necessary self-offering exposes the inadequacy that only Christ would remedy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–24 — The Glory and the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron blesses the people, the glory of the LORD appears, and fire comes from the LORD and consumes the offering. The people shout and fall on their faces.
verseByVerse.theology: God's fire signifies his acceptance of the sacrifice. The appearing of glory evokes both joy and prostrate awe.
verseByVerse.examples: When we grasp that God accepts us in Christ, the only fitting response is joyful, trembling worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: The glory appears "to all the people" — not to priests alone but to the whole redeemed community. The aim of the priesthood was always to bring the people into the radiance of God's presence. In Christ, the veil is torn and all his people behold the glory of God in his face (2 Cor 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fire from God — heaven's seal of acceptance. Sproul: this is the holiness of God breaking into the visible world, and the only possible response is to fall down. Yet they "shouted" too — for the fire fell on the substitute, not on them. This is the gospel's paradox: terror swallowed up in joy, because the consuming fire consumed our Sacrifice in our place.

9.theology:
The goal of worship: glory. All the offerings aim at the appearing of God's glory (9:6, 23), now seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 4:6).

Divine acceptance. The fire from heaven seals God's acceptance of the sacrifice; the fire that fell on the altar fell ultimately on Christ, so it need never fall on us.

Worship in the presence of glory. Shouting joy and prostrate awe together — the fitting response of redeemed sinners who behold God's glory and live.
9.examples:
Then: Israel watched fire flash from God's presence to consume the offering, and the whole nation shouted and fell prostrate — joy and trembling fused in the sight of glory.

Now: Because the fire of judgment fell on Christ, we behold God's glory not in terror but in worship. The right response to grace is still to shout for joy and fall on our faces.

10.title: Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized Fire
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. <sup>2</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. <sup>3</sup>..."Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified."
10.overview:
The same fire that fell in blessing now falls in judgment. Before the smoke of acceptance has cleared, the joy of chapter 9 is shattered. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's own sons, just consecrated to the priesthood, take their censers and offer "unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them" (10:1). And the holy fire that consumed the sacrifice now consumes the priests. They die before the LORD.

This is the most sobering passage in Leviticus, and Sproul's The Holiness of God circles back to it again and again. We instinctively recoil — was the punishment not severe? But Sproul presses us: our shock reveals how little we grasp the holiness of God and how much we presume upon his grace. The wonder is not that Nadab and Abihu died, but that we live. The fire of judgment is the default reality for sinful creatures who approach a holy God on their own terms.

The exact nature of their sin is debated — strange fire not taken from the altar, presumption, perhaps drunkenness (note the prohibition that follows in v. 9). But the heart of it is clear: they approached God in a way "he had not commanded." They presumed to worship on their own terms. And God's verdict is unbending: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified" (10:3). The closer one draws to God, the more his holiness must be honored. Privilege heightens accountability.

How desperately this drives us to Christ. We too have offered unauthorized fire — worship of our own devising, approach on our own terms, presumption upon grace. We have all deserved the fire. But Christ stepped into the place of judgment; the consuming fire fell on him at Calvary. He is the only authorized way to the Father (John 14:6), the new and living way opened through his flesh (Heb 10:20). Nadab and Abihu teach us, with terrible clarity, that there is no casual coming to God — and that the way which is open is open only because Another bore the fire we earned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and are consumed. God declares he will be sanctified among those who draw near.
verseByVerse.theology: God's holiness is not to be trifled with; he must be approached on his terms alone. Privilege heightens accountability.
verseByVerse.examples: Casual, self-styled worship is no light matter. The holiness of God demands reverence and obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Which he had not commanded them" — the indictment in five words. Calvin draws the regulative principle straight from this verse: God will be worshipped not by human invention but by his own appointment. The sin was not gross immorality but presumption — worship on their own terms. Begg warns that the church perennially repeats Nadab's error, offering God fire he has not asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same verb ("consumed," the same fire "from before the LORD") that brought joy in 9:24 now brings death. The line between blessing and judgment is the substitute. Where the fire falls on the offering, there is life; where it falls on the presumptuous worshipper, there is death. Sproul: we are stunned by the severity only because we have grown numb to the holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace.
verseByVerse.commentary: "And Aaron held his peace." The bereaved father's silence is one of the most affecting moments in Scripture — submission to the holiness of God even in unspeakable grief. Ferguson notes that there are times when faith's deepest worship is wordless surrender. "I will be sanctified" — God's holiness will be honored, whether by our reverence or by our judgment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands the priests not to drink wine when entering the tent, that they may distinguish holy from common, clean from unclean, and teach Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who minister to God must be clear-headed and reverent, able to discern holy from common.
verseByVerse.examples: Spiritual leadership demands sobriety and discernment — the ability to distinguish what God hallows from what he does not.

verseByVerse.quote: You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean,
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the priestly vocation in a sentence, and the very heartbeat of Leviticus: to distinguish holy from common. A culture that blurs every distinction cannot worship a holy God. Carson notes that the loss of the categories of holy and common is itself a mark of spiritual decline. The priest must see, and teach others to see, the difference.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses is angry that the sin offering was not eaten, but Aaron's grief-stricken explanation satisfies him.
verseByVerse.theology: Even in a chapter of severe judgment, God makes room for human frailty and grief.
verseByVerse.examples: God is holy, yet tender; he does not break the bruised reed. There is mercy even in the strictest holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron's tender appeal — how could a grieving father feast on the holy day his sons were struck down? — and Moses' acceptance (v. 20) reveal that the God of consuming fire is also the God who does not despise a broken heart (Ps 51:17). Even here, holiness and mercy meet.

10.theology:
The holiness of God. Sproul's great theme: God must be approached on his terms, not ours. The fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu reveals the deadly seriousness of presumptuous worship.

Privilege heightens accountability. 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified' (10:3) — the closer one is brought to God, the more his holiness must be honored.

The only authorized way. There is one acceptable approach to the Father, and it is Christ (John 14:6); the fire we deserved fell on him.
10.examples:
Then: Aaron's sons offered worship of their own devising and were consumed by holy fire; their father stood in silent, submissive grief before the holiness of God.

Now: We are warned against casual, self-styled worship and driven to Christ, the only authorized way to God, who bore in his own body the fire of judgment we deserved.

11.title: Clean and Unclean: A People Set Apart
11.text: <sup>44</sup>For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy... <sup>45</sup>For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
11.overview:
Now begins the section on clean and unclean (chs 11–15), opening with the dietary laws. Which animals may Israel eat, and which not? On the surface these seem arbitrary; in reality they are a daily, table-level catechism in the great theme of separation. Three times a day, at every meal, Israel was reminded that they were a people set apart, that distinctions matter, that the holy and the common are not the same.

Wenham's classic study shows that the categories are not finally about hygiene but about symbolism: the animals that conform to the created order of their domain are clean; the anomalous, the boundary-crossing, the predatory and death-associated are unclean. The clean animal is a living parable of the people who keep within God's appointed bounds. Every meal preached: be distinct, be whole, be set apart unto God.

And the climax of the chapter is the towering refrain that will dominate the rest of Leviticus: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). The dietary laws are not ends in themselves; they serve this. God grounds the call in redemption — "I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (11:45). Holiness is the grateful response of a redeemed people to their redeeming God.

In Christ, the dietary distinctions are fulfilled and lifted. Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), and Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10) abolishes the wall between clean and unclean nations: "What God has made clean, do not call common." The deeper purpose endures — God still calls his people to be holy and distinct — but the boundary now runs not between Jew and Gentile, kosher and non-kosher, but between those who are in Christ and those who are not. Peter himself quotes Leviticus to the church: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet 1:16). The table-level lesson becomes a life-level call.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God distinguishes clean from unclean among land animals, sea creatures, birds, and insects, by criteria of chewing the cud, split hooves, fins, and scales.
verseByVerse.theology: The categories of clean and unclean train Israel in the fundamental distinction between holy and common.
verseByVerse.examples: Daily, ordinary choices were shaped by the call to be distinct. Holiness reaches into the most mundane corners of life.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The laws govern the most ordinary of acts — eating. Begg notes that God claims the kitchen table, the everyday, the routine. Holiness is not confined to the sanctuary; it reaches the dinner plate. Every meal was a small act of obedience and remembrance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–47 — Be Holy, for I Am Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Israel to consecrate themselves and be holy, grounding the call in his own holiness and his act of redemption from Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: The foundational refrain of Leviticus: 'Be holy, for I am holy.' Holiness is grounded in God's character and his redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter applies this directly to the church (1 Pet 1:15-16). The redeemed are called to reflect the holiness of their Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy...
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the heartbeat of the book. The motive for holiness is not fear of punishment but the character of God: "for I am holy." Ferguson observes that biblical holiness is always imitative — we are to be holy because God is, conformed to his likeness. And the indicative grounds the imperative: "I am the LORD your God" — you are mine; therefore be like me.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: Holiness rests on redemption. God does not say "be holy so that I will rescue you" but "I have rescued you; therefore be holy." Grace precedes and grounds obedience. This is the gospel logic that Paul will make explicit: "I appeal to you therefore... by the mercies of God" (Rom 12:1). The redeemed live as the redeemed.

11.theology:
Separation unto God. The dietary laws trained Israel, at every meal, in the distinction between holy and common — a people visibly set apart.

'Be holy, for I am holy.' The defining refrain (11:44-45), grounded in God's character and his redemptive act, quoted by Peter for the church (1 Pet 1:16).

Fulfilled in Christ. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and abolished the Jew-Gentile wall (Acts 10); the call to holiness endures, now defined by union with Christ.
11.examples:
Then: An Israelite, choosing what to eat, was reminded three times a day that he belonged to a holy God and a set-apart people, distinct from the nations around him.

Now: We are no longer bound by kosher laws, but the call to be holy and distinct is heightened in Christ. 'As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct' (1 Pet 1:15).

12.title: Purification After Childbirth: The Offering of the Poor
12.text: <sup>6</sup>And when the days of her purifying are completed... she shall bring to the priest... a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering... <sup>8</sup>And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons...
12.overview:
This brief chapter addresses purification after childbirth. To modern sensibilities it can seem strange, even offensive — why should the joyful, God-ordained act of bringing forth life render a woman ceremonially unclean? But we must read it within Leviticus's symbolic world. The issue is not that childbirth is sinful, but that it involves the flow of blood, and blood is life, and the loss of life-fluid touches the deep biblical association between fallenness, mortality, and the need for cleansing. Every birth, since Eden, comes trailing the shadow of the curse — "in pain you shall bring forth children" (Gen 3:16) — and every new life born is a life born into a world of sin and death, needing redemption.

Wenham notes that the purification ritual does not stigmatize motherhood; it dignifies it by drawing it into the sphere of God's holiness. The mother brings a burnt offering and a sin offering, and is pronounced clean. The wonder of birth is honored, and the reality of a fallen world is acknowledged, both at once.

But the chapter's deepest glory shines in the New Testament. For Luke records that Mary and Joseph fulfilled exactly this law for the infant Jesus: "And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses... they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord... and to offer a sacrifice... 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons'" (Luke 2:22–24). Two birds — the offering specifically appointed in 12:8 for those who could not afford a lamb. The offering of the poor.

Stop and feel the weight of it. The Lamb of God himself was brought to the temple, and for him was offered the poor woman's two birds — because the Holy Family could not afford a lamb. They did not need to buy a lamb; they were carrying him. The Maker of heaven and earth entered our world in such poverty that his mother brought the cheapest legal offering. "Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9). Leviticus 12, fulfilled in a Bethlehem-born baby, becomes one of the tenderest gospel windows in all the Old Testament.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After childbirth a woman is ceremonially unclean for a set period, with circumcision of a son on the eighth day.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the holy act of birth, in a fallen world, is touched by the need for cleansing — every life is born into sin's shadow.
verseByVerse.examples: We enter the world needing redemption from our first breath. 'In sin did my mother conceive me' (Ps 51:5) is not about the act but the condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eighth day brings the covenant sign of circumcision — and on the eighth day the infant Jesus was circumcised and named (Luke 2:21). He who would establish the new covenant submitted to the sign of the old, fulfilling all righteousness on our behalf from his earliest days.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — The Offering, and the Provision for the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mother brings a lamb and a bird; but if she cannot afford a lamb, two birds suffice. Atonement is made and she is clean.
verseByVerse.theology: God scales the offering to the worshipper's poverty; atonement is never priced out of reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary brought the offering of the poor for Jesus (Luke 2:24) — the King of glory entered the world in poverty for our sake.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the days of her purifying are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering...
verseByVerse.commentary: The standard offering was a lamb plus a bird. Calvin notes that God thus drew the most intimate, domestic moments of life into the orbit of worship — even the nursery is not outside his holy claim.

verseByVerse.quote: And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the offering Mary brought (Luke 2:24). Begg loves to dwell here: the Lamb of God was carried in the arms of a mother too poor to buy a lamb. The infinite riches of heaven entered our poverty so completely that the cheapest legal offering was made for him. "For your sake he became poor" (2 Cor 8:9). Grace stoops to the lowest, and the King is found among the poor.

12.theology:
Born into a fallen world. Even the joy of birth, marked by blood, points to the universal need for cleansing — every life enters the shadow of sin and death.

Atonement scaled to poverty. The provision of two birds for the poor (12:8) shows that no one is shut out from God by want.

The poverty of Christ. Mary's offering of two birds (Luke 2:24) reveals that the Lamb of God entered the world in real poverty — 'for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9).
12.examples:
Then: A new mother in Israel, after the appointed days, brought her offering — a lamb if she could, two birds if she could not — and was pronounced clean before the LORD.

Now: We marvel that Mary brought the offering of the poor for the Son of God. The King of glory met us in poverty; let no one think themselves too lowly for his grace.

13.title: Skin Disease: The Priest Who Examines
13.text: <sup>2</sup>When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest... <sup>45</sup>The leprous person... shall cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.' <sup>46</sup>...He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the long, painstaking law of tsara'at — usually translated "leprosy," though it covers a range of skin conditions and even mold in fabrics. The priest is appointed as the examiner, the one who looks closely, declares clean or unclean, and pronounces the verdict. The detail is exhausting precisely because the stakes are so high: a wrong diagnosis means either a clean person banished or an unclean person spreading defilement through the camp.

The disease becomes, in Scripture's symbolic vocabulary, the great picture of sin: it spreads, it disfigures, it works beneath the surface and erupts visibly, it isolates, and it makes one unfit for the presence of God. The verdict "unclean" carries a terrible weight — the leper must tear his clothes, cover his lip, cry "Unclean, unclean," and live alone outside the camp (13:45–46). Cut off from worship, from family, from community — a living picture of the alienation that sin works.

Sproul and Ferguson both draw the line: this is what sin does to the soul. It defiles, it spreads, it cuts off from God and others, and no amount of self-cleansing can reverse it. The leper could not heal himself; he could only be examined and declared. The priest's verdict was final and the sentence was exile.

And here the heart aches for the Great Priest who is coming. For the law could only diagnose; it could not cure. The priest could declare a leper unclean but could not make him clean. Then came One who, when a leper fell before him crying "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean," stretched out his hand and touched him — the unthinkable, defiling touch — and said, "I will; be clean" (Matt 8:2–3). He did not become unclean by the touch; the leper became clean. The Great High Priest both examines and heals, both pronounces the verdict and bears it away. Where Aaron could only send the leper outside the camp, Jesus "suffered outside the gate" (Heb 13:12) to bring the outcast home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priest examines skin afflictions, quarantines doubtful cases, and pronounces clean or unclean.
